title: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly (2007)
summary: An antitrust complaint needed factual allegations plausibly suggesting an agreement; parallel conduct consistent with independent action was insufficient.
notes:
Do not substitute the summary-judgment test for this pleading inquiry. Matsushita also discusses inferences about antitrust conspiracies, but it addresses an evidentiary record at a later procedural stage.

Justice Souter wrote for a 7-2 Court; the plaintiffs were subscribers of local telephone and high-speed internet service suing the incumbent local exchange carriers under section 1 of the Sherman Act, and the opinion retired Conley v. Gibson's 'no set of facts' formulation, requiring instead enough facts to state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face; Justice Ginsburg joined the Stevens dissent except as to Part IV.

sections.Parties: Telephone-service customers sued incumbent local exchange carriers, alleging a conspiracy in violation of the Sherman Act.
sections.Material Facts: After the statutory changes intended to open local telephone markets to competition, the complaint alleged that the incumbent carriers resisted entry by new competitors and refrained from competing in one another’s territories. It treated their parallel conduct as evidence of an agreement. The alleged acts also fit the individual economic incentives of each incumbent. The complaint’s general statements that the carriers had conspired did not add facts about how an agreement arose or why the parallel behavior indicated one.
sections.Procedural History: The district court dismissed the complaint. The Second Circuit reversed under its reading of the permissive pleading standard. The Supreme Court reversed the court of appeals, holding the allegations insufficient.
sections.Issue: Did allegations of parallel conduct, accompanied by general assertions of conspiracy, plausibly state the agreement required by antitrust law?
sections.Holding: No. The complaint had to include enough factual matter to suggest an agreement, rather than merely conduct consistent with one.
sections.Reasoning: The majority distinguished the possibility of unlawful agreement from a factual basis plausibly supporting it. It accepted the described parallel acts for pleading purposes but concluded that those acts did not themselves point to concerted action rather than independent business choices. A legal label could not perform that missing inferential work. The Court expressly rejected continued reliance on Conley’s no-set-of-facts formulation, while explaining that the plaintiff did not have to show a probability of success or prove the claim at filing. Discovery costs mattered to the majority because a largely ungrounded claim could produce expensive proceedings and settlement pressure before the absence of an agreement became clear.

learning.why: An antitrust complaint needed factual allegations plausibly suggesting an agreement; parallel conduct consistent with independent action was insufficient.

topics.cp-plausibility: Parallel conduct and an assertion of agreement did not supply facts plausibly suggesting the required conspiracy.
topics.cp-pleading-proof: Plausibility was a threshold for proceeding, not a requirement to prove an agreement at filing.
topics.cp-access: The majority considered the expense of discovery and pressure to settle insufficiently grounded claims.
topics.cp-precedent: The Court expressly retired Conley’s no-set-of-facts formulation.
topics.cp-notice-pleading: Twombly retired Conley's 'no set of facts' formulation, the touchstone of notice pleading.
topics.cp-frcp-8: The plausibility standard is a construction of Rule 8(a)(2)'s 'short and plain statement' requirement.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Stevens, joined in relevant part by Justice Ginsburg, disputed the treatment of the complaint and emphasized notice pleading, the alleged agreement, and the ability to control discovery. The disagreement concerns both what the allegations communicated and when costly factual investigation should become available.

mnemonic.rationale: Telephone carriers who did not compete
